newsitem.title: USA: Dow slides 160 points on rising interest rate fears. [CORRECTED 00:10 GMT 14/3]
newsitem.headline: Dow slides 160 points on rising interest rate fears. [CORRECTED 00:10 GMT 14/3]

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 160 points on Thursday in a massive sell-off after robust February retail sales data rekindled fears the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates soon.
The Dow index fell 160.48 points to close at 6,878.89 (corrects Dow closing level) -- the fifth steepest fall in point terms in the history of the average.
The decline of 2.28 percent, however, ranks nowhere near the top percentage losses.
Broader indexes were also sharply lower, with losers trouncing gainers 2,070 to 510 on heavy volume of 503.7 million on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts cited a stiff bond market sell-off as the primary catalyst for stocks' decline. The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury fell nearly a full point to drive the yield up to 6.96 percent, its highest level in nearly six months, from Wednesday's close of 6.88 percent.

The Fed's interest rate policy meeting on March 25 has been a major concern that has weighed on financial markets recently. On Thursday, however, investors no longer seemed uncertain about the meeting's outcome, analysts said.
"The market, in both bonds and stocks, is telling us a rate rise is a foregone conclusion," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.

Until Thursday, blue-chip stocks had continued their rise with only momentary lapses despite a steady rise in long-term bond interest rates. Now with rates near 7 percent, however, analysts said the rally suddenly appeared suspect.

"We really haven't seen much reason for improvement and yet stock prices have gone up," said Melissa Brown, director of quantitative research at Prudential Securities. "When stocks are overvalued and rates go up, that tends to magnify the issue."
Financial and transportation issues were hard hit, as both are particularly sensitive to interest rate changes.
The session's heaviest selling was reserved for a group with problems all their own: the tobacco stocks.
News that the Mississippi Supreme Court rejected a challenge to the state's Medicaid suit against tobacco companies sent tobacco stocks skidding.

Philip Morris Cos Inc. tumbled 10-3/4 to 126, although about 1-1/4 of the decline reflected a dividend-related adjustment. The shares contributed roughly a fifth of the overall loss posted by the Dow. RJR Nabisco Holdings Inc. fell 2-7/8 to 33-1/4.
Analysts said blue chips would likely remain hostage to higher rates at least until the Fed meeting.

"The bond market isn't going to turn around until we get a sense of where the economy actually stands and what (Fed Chairman) Alan Greenspan is thinking," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
Even so, few see the bull market's demise at hand.
"The bull market is still intact," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co. "This is a correction just like any other and we feel it's going to bottom fairly quickly."
The market will get little chance to breathe. A major inflation indicator -- the February Producer Price Index -- is due before the stock market opens on Friday.

The report has consistently failed to show inflation building at the wholesale level and indeed, economists expect a 0.1 percent drop in wholesale prices for February vs. a 0.3 percent decline in January.
Citicorp fell 5-1/2 to 117-1/4 and Chase Manhattan Corp. shed 4-3/4 to 99-1/8 amid the broad decline in financial stocks.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 10.85 points to 1,293.28.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks fell 14.70 points to 789.56.
The American Stock Exchange index was off 4.02 at 598.02.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 7.67 to 415.87. The average price per share fell 79 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,553.127, down 122.165, or 1.59 percent.
